newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong civil liberties amendments to go to vote.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong civil liberties amendments to go to vote.

text.p: Controversial amendments to Hong Kong civil liberties laws are expected to be submitted on Saturday for approval by the territory's future interim legislature, a spokesman for the chamber said on Tuesday.

The proposed amendments, which restrict demonstrations and ban overseas funding of political parties, have drawn a storm of protest from Hong Kong's active pro-democracy lobby and the outgoing British colonial administration.
The democracy lobby plans to contest in court any laws passed by the China-installed Provisional Legislature, arguing that the body itself is unconstitutional.
The final details of the amendments are expected to be fine-tuned by future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa's inner cabinet on Tuesday.
If all goes according to plan, they will be published on Thursday ahead of the Provisional Legislature's meeting on Saturday.
The legislature, selected in December, meets across the border in the Chinese city of Shenzhen to avoid triggering any legal challenges for operating in Hong Kong.
It will replace the existing elected chamber when Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30.

Tung's aides have said the incoming government is looking to soften but not scrap some of the original amendment proposals following a three-week public consultation exercise which yielded more than 6,000 submissions.
Local newspapers speculated that Tung's administration may relax the requirement that people planning to hold demonstrations obtain police permission seven days in advance.
They said the period may be shortened to 48 or even 24 hours and the requirement might be waived entirely in special circumstances.

The definition of a political organisation is expected to be re-defined to exclude labour organisations and religious bodies, some papers said, and a ban on overseas donations would not apply to China but would apply to China's rival Taiwan.
A Tung spokesman declined to comment on specifics.
Concessions are unlikely to mollify Hong Kong's pro- democracy activists, who have lobbied against the amendments, angering Tung who accused them of "badmouthing" Hong Kong.
Tung is not expected to undertake any overseas visits until well after the handover, now 49 days away.
The centrist Ming Pao newspaper said on Tuesday there was no need to tighten Hong Kong's existing ordinances.
The sentencing on Monday of three activists for storming the Japanese consulate last October showed the legal system was sufficient to control demonstrations, the paper said.
"It had struck a balance between the freedom of assembly and social stability," it said.
The three activists were members of a pressure group protesting against the landing by Japanese rightists on a chain of uninhabited islands claimed by Beijing, Tokyo and Taipei.
They were fined HK$4,000 (US$500) each and ordered to pay costs of HK$2,000 ($250).

Tung has said his amendments were needed to prevent a repeat of such lawlessness and has argued that his restrictions were no more onerous than those in some Western countries and merely return Hong Kong laws to where they were before a Bill of Rights ordinance was passed in 1991.

Singapore's elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew urged Tung in an interview with the Financial Times on Tuesday to scrap all political reforms instigated by Governor Chris Patten to win the confidence of the Chinese leadership.
Patten's mild democratic reforms angered China, which responded by drawing up plans to install the interim provisional legislature for a year until new elections are held.
